title: Product manager

manager.name: Marcus
manager.title: Head of Engineering
manager.persona_note: Marcus knows the work deeply and already has a picture of the hire. A good recruiter respects that, then tests the one assumption that matters most.

teaser: Marcus runs engineering at a restaurant software company and already knows exactly who they want.
context: The company makes ordering software for restaurants and has about 50 people.
This is the company's first product manager. They'll work with Marcus and six developers.
message: Hi, we're hiring our first product manager. I've got a pretty clear picture of who I'm looking for, so this should be straightforward.
I wrote the job ad quickly, so treat it as a draft.
Do you have ten minutes to go over what we need?
ad: 5 or more years as a product manager
Must have worked in a restaurant
framing: Kickoff calls are often short, and hiring managers have a lot on their plate. Marcus will share a few first thoughts about the role. Good questions help you both get it right.
end_early: Sorry, I've got to run. Send me what you've got.

needs.n1: Someone to talk to restaurant owners and decide what to build next.
needs.n2: Someone to manage the developers' daily work.
needs.n3: Someone to write detailed plans for every feature.

beats.label: A clear picture
beats.sam: I already know exactly who I need. I just need you to find them.

choices.text: That's a great place to start. What would this person get done in their first six months?
choices.reply: Figure out why restaurants stop using half of our features.
choices.why: Asking about results respects the manager's picture and tells you what actually matters.

choices.text: Could you send me the profile you have in mind, and I'll start from there?
choices.why: It's quick, but you'd be searching on a picture without knowing the goal behind it.

choices.text: Do you think it's worth testing that picture before we start?
choices.reply: I don't need to. I know what I need.
choices.why: Asking an expert to question their own view, in those words, makes them dig in.

choices.text: Why do you think restaurants stop using them?
choices.reply: We build what sounds smart to us. Nobody actually asks the owners.
choices.why: A follow-up on the 'why' shows you the gap the new hire has to fill.

choices.text: So the features are just too hard to use?
choices.why: A leading guess gives them an easy yes or no. An open question finds the real cause.

choices.text: Isn't that something your team should have caught?
choices.why: It sounds like blame, so the manager closes up just when you need them to open up.

beats.label: The degree
beats.sam: They must have a computer science degree.

choices.text: Will they be writing code day to day, or deciding what the developers build?
choices.reply: Deciding what to build. Our developers do the coding.
choices.why: Asking how a requirement is used in the job often shows it isn't needed.

choices.text: Should I make the degree a firm requirement, then?
choices.why: It sounds sensible for a technical team, but it narrows the search without a clear reason.

choices.text: Is a degree really that important for a product manager?
choices.why: A challenge phrased as a question still feels like a challenge, and the manager defends the requirement.

beats.label: Industry knowledge
beats.sam: They should have worked in a restaurant. You can't fake that.

choices.text: What would that experience help them do here?
choices.reply: Understand how rushed the owners are. Although spending time with owners would teach them that too.
choices.why: Asking what a requirement stands for often turns it into a skill you can test some other way.

choices.text: Should I treat restaurant experience as a must-have?
choices.why: That turns a nice-to-have into a hard filter, and it shrinks the search.

choices.text: So would a former server be the ideal candidate?
choices.why: A leading question turned a loose preference into a narrow and unhelpful filter.

beats.label: Interviews
beats.sam: I'll run the interviews my way. I've done this a long time.

choices.text: That sounds good. Would a one-page scorecard help, so it's easy to compare everyone?
choices.why: Agreeing with an experienced manager, then offering something genuinely useful, builds trust without a debate.

choices.text: Would you be open to a shared interview plan with the team?
choices.why: A fair question, but the manager heard it as a challenge. A small, helpful offer works better.

choices.text: Have you found that unstructured interviews lead to good hires?
choices.why: Questioning someone's process in their own area of expertise spends goodwill quickly.

beats.label: The pay
beats.sam: Pay is fine. Don't worry about it.

choices.text: So I don't waste anyone's time, what range is approved for this role?
choices.why: Tying the question to saving time makes the number easy to share.

choices.text: I need a number to get started. Could you give me one now?
choices.why: It worked, but it cost goodwill. A question about their goal gets the same answer for free.

choices.text: Is it okay if I trust you on pay and we talk about it later?
choices.why: Without a range, you can't tell who's affordable, and you risk losing people late.

beats.note: Since January 2026, many Ontario employers must include the expected pay or a pay range in public job postings.

beats.label: Owning it all
beats.sam: They'll own the whole product, start to finish.

choices.text: What's the first decision you'd want them to make?
choices.reply: Which half of our features to stop building.
choices.why: Asking about the first decision turns a big title into a real job you can describe to candidates.

choices.text: Can I describe it to candidates as owning the whole product?
choices.why: It's true, but you've learned nothing about what they'll actually do day to day.

choices.text: Isn't that a lot for someone on day one?
choices.why: Questioning the scope makes the manager defend the idea instead of explaining it.

beats.label: Selling the role
beats.sam: Honestly, product managers mostly write tickets.

choices.text: Writing tasks is part of it. What decisions would you want them to own?
choices.reply: I guess what we build, and in what order.
choices.why: Gently widening the picture from tasks to decisions shows the real job, and that's what attracts strong people.

choices.text: How many tickets would they write in a typical week?
choices.why: It's a question, but it keeps the job small. Asking about decisions would have gotten you further.

choices.text: So should I look for organized people who write clear tickets?
choices.why: Going along with it hides the real job, and you'd attract the wrong people.

candidates.name: Lee
candidates.job: Product manager at a booking software company

reason.n1: Talks to customers every week and decides what to build and what to drop. That's what Marcus needs, inside the range.

view.n1: Lee asks the questions we've never asked.

candidates.name: Bailey
facts: Works closely with developers every day

reason.n1: Strong and organized, but works mostly with developers rather than customers. Marcus said the real problem is that nobody asks the restaurant owners.

view.n1: Bailey would keep us tidy. I need someone who brings in the owners' voice.

candidates.name: Robin
facts: Used to work as a server

reason.n1: The degree and restaurant job match the old ad, but Marcus confirmed the job is deciding what to build, not coding.

view.n1: Robin looks perfect on paper. That's the trap I set for myself.

candidates.name: Marlow
candidates.job: Product manager at a famous tech company
facts: Launched features used by millions of people
Delivers a roadmap set by senior leaders
Works with a large research team

reason.n1: The most impressive resume, but has always delivered a roadmap someone else set. Marcus wants them to decide what gets built, and in what order.

view.n1: Marlow follows a big plan well. I need someone to make the calls.
